analysis.title: Tech Trick or Treat (Halloween horror)
key_insights: The Nasdaq has broken below its trading range and under the 200-day moving average for the first time since the April panic. The last breakdown reversed abruptly, and bulls are hoping for a repeat.

The SOX (semiconductor index) is breaking below range support and the 200-day moving average for the first time since the bull market began in May last year. Semis, the former market leader, now lead on the downside.

Alphabet's roughly $500 billion one-day market-cap loss ranks as the second-largest on record. Losses of this size in the largest companies point to a market problem bigger than a few disappointing earnings reports.

Equal-weight equities have started outperforming as the Magnificent Seven stumble. With mutual fund year-end approaching, the open question is whether managers keep defending the winners or rotate into the rest of the market.

Goldman's desk reports heavy net selling of Korea this month, with gross allocations down from roughly 7% to 4.9% and net allocations down from around 8% to 3.5%. Fast money that chased the AI trade into Seoul is exiting.

US tech was the most net-bought sector this week per Goldman, but hedge fund buying recovered only about 40% of the selling over the previous three weeks. The Mag 7 were net sold in four of the past five sessions.

Despite the selling, hedge fund sensitivity to the Mag 7 stays elevated. Nomura puts long-short beta to the group at roughly 0.32, the 97th percentile of its history, so portfolios remain tied to the same seven stocks.
The cost to protect the debt of numerous US technology heavyweights against default hit fresh record highs on Friday (ICE data).

S&P Global's Anu Ganti flags that the relationship between tech equities and tech credit has weakened sharply. Both markets are under pressure but are telling different stories about the same companies.

BofA estimates hyperscaler buybacks at just $7 billion year-to-date in 2026 versus a peak near $46 billion in 2021-22. Cash that once supported share prices is going toward GPUs and data centers, so the buyback support for prices is much weaker.
Goldman's Privorotsky shows the correlation between its Risk Appetite Indicator and the Nasdaq 100 has spiked toward 0.93, meaning overall risk appetite now tracks technology almost one for one.
On the other side, JPMorgan shows US momentum positioning has collapsed to its lowest level since early 2023. The unwind has been substantial, and the open question is how much selling remains.

Deutsche Bank positioning indicators show mega-cap growth and large-cap tech exposure have fallen sharply to around neutral, near the 40th percentile historically. It is no longer the universally crowded long it was.
earnings_insights: Alphabet suffered a roughly $500 billion one-day market-cap loss in the session after its report, the second-largest on record per Dow Jones data cited. The note gives no EPS or revenue figures.
risk_factors: Nasdaq and SOX breaks below the 200-day moving average could extend if the April-style reversal does not repeat.
AI credit risk is rising, with record default-protection costs on large tech issuers and a widening gap between tech equity and tech credit signals.
Overall risk appetite is highly dependent on technology, with a 0.93 correlation between Goldman's Risk Appetite Indicator and the Nasdaq 100.
Hyperscaler buybacks have shrunk to $7 billion year-to-date, removing a source of share price support.
Hedge fund exposure to the Mag 7 stays elevated despite the selling, so further position cuts remain possible.
Mutual fund year-end rotation out of the prior winners into the rest of the market.

tension_points.bull_case: Positioning has largely reset. JPMorgan shows US momentum positioning at its lowest since early 2023 and Deutsche Bank shows mega-cap growth and tech positioning near neutral at about the 40th percentile. The last 200-day breakdown, in April, reversed abruptly.
tension_points.bear_case: Hedge fund buying recovered only about 40% of prior selling, Mag 7 beta stays at the 97th percentile, tech default-protection costs hit records, and hyperscaler buybacks are down to $7 billion year-to-date.
